papers.title: Aging as Cross-Hallmark Obstruction Amplification:A Sheaf-Theoretic Model of Repair Closure, Senescence, Inflammation, and Regenerative Failure
papers.authors: Juan Segura
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Aging is usually described as the accumulation of molecular, cellular, tissue, and systemic defects. The twelve-hallmark framework has made this description biologically precise, but it still leaves open a structural question: why do heterogeneous defects begin to behave as one organism-level loss of repair capacity? Aging is formalized as loss of autopoietic repair closure in a sheaf-theoretic model. The central claim is that aging is not the negation of life, but the narrowing of the space in which a living system can repair, regenerate, and preserve its own organization. Each hallmark is represented as a local-to-global constraint layer over a tissue, cellular, or organismal complex. Viable self-maintenance corresponds to global sections; unresolved incompatibilities correspond to cohomological obstructions; repair failure is tracked by persistence under injury, stress, or regeneration filtrations. The twelve hallmarks are coupled by an extension whose connecting morphism measures when coherent regulatory or interface states generate material-repair incompatibilities. The main formal result is an exact repair-reserve decomposition: organismal repair reserve equals material-repair closure plus regulatory-interface closure minus cross-hallmark obstruction rank. A categorical layer complements this result: by the Yoneda principle, aging is visible as deformation of the complete experimental response profile, while senescence is represented as an idempotent cellular retract. Further results show that cross-hallmark interactions amplify obstruction rank beyond isolated hallmark effects; aged systems can remain viable at baseline while losing repair closure under challenge; and local improvement of one hallmark is not equivalent to organismal rejuvenation unless it expands the benign repair-control kernel. A computable senescence--inflammation--stem-cell model illustrates the theory through rank regimes, repair barcodes, and a phase diagram. Aging becomes measurable as loss of gluing capacity across the biological layers that sustain autopoietic self-maintenance.</jats:p>

papers.title: Generative models of living development: an interaction-centered proposal and its implications for artificial life research
papers.authors: Bin Yin; Xiao-Rui Wu
papers.abstract: Artificial life and integrative systems neuroscience increasingly seek to explain how agency is organized through development, not merely how an already-formed controller optimizes a predefined task. This article advances an interaction-centered theory that links computational generative models, which infer hidden causes and candidate action policies, with experimental ecologies, which generate the developmental histories to be explained. The framework distinguishes reward and prior preference from concern, normativity, habit, and action policy. Concerns denote system-relative dimensions of regulatory significance grounded in an agent's organization; habits are historically acquired dispositions; and action policies remain formally defined candidates within a computational model. The code-mediated concern hypothesis proposes that events acquire functional significance when adaptor-implemented mappings make cues informative about viability-linked concerns, thereby changing inference, precision, habit, and action selection. Teleonomic and organizational accounts locate the normative force of these concerns in present self-maintaining organization rather than conscious design or backward causation. The Layered Model of Agency differentiates operative, reflective, joint, material-mediated, sign-mediated, and symbolic agency, preventing evidence for low-level control from being generalized to collective, artifact-mediated, symbolic, or phenomenal agency. The Human-Rat Interaction Paradigm (HRIP) supplies an extensible experimental architecture for studying how structured human-rat interaction histories shape multidomain developmental trajectories. The inaugural male-rat study permits only sex-specific inference; the broader HRIP paradigm accommodates female, male, and mixed-sex samples in comparative and mechanistic research designs. Six propositions and eight predictions define tests of model comparison, cue remapping and adaptor perturbation, habit-policy dissociation, reciprocal coupling, material and sign mediation, multimodal trajectories, developmental and sex moderation, and layer-specific evidence. Together, these elements define a testable program for developmental artificial life while preserving the distinction between functional agency-like organization and phenomenal agency.
papers.categories: Generative grammar; Cognitive science; Agency (philosophy); Action (physics); Normative

papers.title: Towards origins of virtual artificial life: an overview
papers.authors: Susan Stepney
papers.abstract: The field of artificial life (ALife) studies 'life as it could be', in contrast to biology's study of 'life as we know it to be'. This includes a wide range of potential physical substrates, from synthetic biology (new genes), through xenobiology (new amino acids and DNA bases), inorganic chemistry (different structural elements), soft and hard robotics (new kinds of bodies) and also virtual life (existing inside a computer). Since any such life forms are artificial, the originating mechanisms can be similarly artificial, or can attempt to emulate natural mechanisms. Given the wide range of possible substrates and origins, it is crucial to have good definitions, and well-defined ways to detect and measure life, if and when it originates. This overview examines the current state of the art in ALife in defining, detecting and originating its subject matter, with its main focus on virtual life. After discussing common properties of several definitions of life, the overview synthesizes an engineering-focussed definition, in terms of abstract requirements, generic designs and specific implementation mechanisms, and then reviews the current state of the art through this lens. Although virtual ALife that satisfies all these requirements is yet to be exhibited, significant progress has been made on engineering individual mechanisms and, arguably, partially alive systems.This article is part of the theme issue 'Origins of life: the possible and the actual'.
papers.categories: Artificial life; Computer science; Theme (computing); Artificial intelligence; Field (mathematics)

papers.title: Genealogies of organizational closure: from logical paradox to mind in life
papers.authors: Sergio Rubin; Andrea Roli; Pasquale Stano; Luisa Damiano
papers.abstract: Organizational closure occupies a central position in contemporary theories of autonomy, anticipation, agency, sense making, and the continuity between life and mind. Its investigation has given rise to a diverse landscape of related explanations, including closure to information, cyclic closure, operational closure, semantic closure, closure-to-efficient causation, metabolic closure, and closure of constraints. Although each of these explanatory approaches captures important aspects of organizational closure, their proliferation has often generated conceptual ambiguity. As a result, organizational closure is frequently conflated with feedback loops, recursive algorithms, self-organization, or biochemical cycles. This paper develops a genealogical conceptual analysis of the research programs from which these various accounts emerged, tracing their origins across mathematical logic, first- and second-order cybernetics, general systems theory, thermodynamics, metabolic theory, relational biology, and the biology of cognition. In doing so, it provides a principled framework for assessing the commitments involved whenever a notion of closure is invoked, while clarifying the origins of these explanations and the relations among them. Particular attention is devoted to the roles of self-reference, circular causality, replication maps, semantics, free energy, automata, operations, and constraints in shaping the current understanding of organizational closure. On this basis, the study advances the interpretative thesis that organizational closure is most coherently understood as a circular organization of efficient causes through which living beings continuously produce and maintain the conditions of their own existence. From this perspective, organizational closure appears irreducible to purely algorithmic descriptions inherited from the Church-Turing thesis-not because living beings cannot be simulated in specific respects, but because the causal production of the conditions of their own realization cannot be exhaustively characterized as a state-determined syntactic procedure. This interpretation helps clarify the distinctions between organizational closure and the notions with which it is often conflated, while providing a framework for assessing current debates concerning artificial intelligence, large language models (LLMs), semantic meaning, and sense making in the face of ambiguity and logical paradox.
papers.categories: Closure (psychology); Epistemology; Conflation; Sociology; Organizational studies

papers.title: Substrate-Coupled Artificial Life: From Virtual Origins to Physical Silicon
papers.authors: Daniel Grachov
papers.abstract: Artificial life studies life-like organisation across possible substrates, and classifies its bottom-up systems by where the artificial organism appears: in a physico-chemical, physico-mechanical, or computational medium. We argue that this taxonomy leaves a second axis underspecified, the causal role of the computing substrate itself, and that the omission carries a cost. The stakes of this missing axis are visible in the field’s recent stocktaking: virtual artificial life has not yet exhibited a system that satisfies the full requirements of life (autopoiesis, agency, and open-ended adaptation), with thermodynamic abstraction and the brittleness of symbolic substrates recurring as limitations (Stepney, 2025). We propose substrate-coupled artificial life (SCAL) as a research programme in which the physical dynamics of the substrate participate causally in the production, persistence, and adaptation of life-like organisation, rather than serving as an inert execution layer. The framework is grounded in three observations about conventional silicon: 1/f noise from charge-trap dynamics at MOSFET interfaces, a cache-hierarchy latency gradient that satisfies Lewontin-style criteria for differential persistence among self-reinforcing memory-topology structures, and DRAM operating far from equilibrium as a Prigogine-class dissipative structure. We specify the experimental requirements such a programme implies in conventional silicon and set out specific falsification criteria. The work is theoretical and pre-experimental: it defines the framework, identifies the experimental commitments required to test it, and specifies the conditions under which it would fail.
papers.categories: Artificial life; Dissipative system; Abstraction; Computer science; Adaptation (eye)

papers.title: Substrate-Coupled Artificial Life: From Virtual Origins to Physical Silicon
papers.authors: Daniel Grachov
papers.abstract: Artificial life studies life-like organisation across substrates. The standard bottom-up taxonomy distinguishes physico-chemical, physico-mechanical, and computational substrates (Stepney, 2025), and classifies where an artificial organism appears. A recent overview of virtual artificial life (Stepney, 2025) concludes that virtual systems satisfying the full requirements of life (autopoiesis, agency, and open-ended adaptation) have not yet been exhibited, and identifies thermodynamic abstraction and the brittleness of symbolic substrates as recurrent limitations. We argue that an axis orthogonal to the standard taxonomy has remained underspecified: the causal role of the computing substrate itself. We propose substrate-coupled artificial life (SCAL) as a research programme in which the physical dynamics of the substrate participate causally in the production, persistence, and adaptation of life-like organisation, rather than serving as an inert execution layer. The framework is grounded in three observations about conventional silicon: 1/f noise from charge-trap dynamics at MOSFET interfaces, a cache-hierarchy latency gradient that satisfies Lewontin-style criteria for differential persistence among self-reinforcing memory-topology structures, and DRAM operating far from equilibrium as a Prigogine-class dissipative structure. We specify the experimental requirements such a programme implies in conventional silicon and set out specific falsification criteria. The work is theoretical and pre-experimental: it defines the framework, identifies the experimental commitments required to test it, and specifies the conditions under which it would fail.

papers.title: Repairing the defective folding of alpha-sarcoglycan is needed to promote myogenic cell engraftment in 3D artificial muscle models of LGMDR3
papers.authors: Edoardo Maghin; Alberto Benetollo; Martina Scano; Paola Caccin; Eugenia Carraro; Martina Piccoli; Dorianna Sandonà
papers.abstract: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy 2D (or LGMDR3) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SGCA gene, which encode α-sarcoglycan (α-SG). α-SG is a critical component of the dystrophin-associated protein complex, whose role in differentiated muscle is to distribute contraction force and protect the sarcolemma from mechanical damage. Most SGCA mutations are missense, leading to a folding-defective α-SG that is degraded by the ubiquitin-proteasome system, destabilizing the sarcolemma and causing progressive muscle weakness. Notably, pharmacological restoration of α-SG function using cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) correctors, such as C17, can rescue the SG-complex, improving muscle strength in an LGMDR3 mouse model. Our initial aim was to generate 3D diaphragm-like models of LGMDR3 by seeding patient-derived myoblasts onto a decellularised diaphragm scaffold, thereby mimicking the disease environment and enabling drug screening beyond the limitations of 2D cultures. While the models did not behave as anticipated, the unexpected outcome led us to uncover a previously underappreciated role of α-SG. Specifically, we found that α-SG expressed by immature myoblasts is crucial for cell adhesion and migration, key processes for muscle development, regeneration, and successful engraftment into a decellularized extracellular matrix. These processes, compromised in LGMDR3 cells, can be rescued through CFTR correctors, further supporting their potential therapeutic application in LGMDR3.
papers.categories: Sarcolemma; Cell biology; Decellularization; Myocyte; Muscular dystrophy

papers.title: OpenLife: Toward Open-World Artificial Life with Autonomous LLM Agents
papers.authors: Atsushi Masumori; Itsuki Doi; Norihiro Maruyama; Ryosuke Takata; Takashi Ikegami
papers.abstract: Artificial life has explored life-like behavior on many computational substrates, but mostly in researcher-designed closed worlds. We argue that large language model (LLM) agents—with persistent memory, tool use, and network access—now make it possible to move artificial life into the open social, technical, and economic world, a paradigm we call open-world Artificial Life (open-world ALIFE). Our proof-of-concept, OpenLife, gives an otherwise stateless LLM a persistent memory organized by meaning and a learning loop that appraises its own experience in open vocabulary rather than by scalar reward, so it grows from experience under a budget-based metabolism that makes persistence normative. Running six such agents in the open world for about twelve weeks, we report the life-like dynamics that emerge: a shift from reactive to spontaneous activity, individuation into distinct agents, emergent social structure, and a first self-earned external income. Autonomy is not automation: an LLM left to itself is far weaker at finding the problems that serve its own persistence than at solving those handed to it. We do not claim OpenLife has realized artificial life, but that open-world ALIFE is now a viable experimental paradigm and a concrete platform for studying what might be called living AI.
papers.categories: Artificial life; Artificial intelligence; Computer science; Cognitive science; Meaning (existential)

papers.title: Posterior Matching Distillation
papers.authors: Hidir Yesiltepe; Julius Berner; Arash Vahdat; Pinar Yanardag
papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

papers.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
papers.authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral; Kaan Oktay; Alec Helbling; Atakan Kara; Duen Horng Chau; Pinar Yanardag
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

papers.title: AnyVIO: Feed-Forward Streaming Visual-Inertial Odometry Across Platforms
papers.authors: Omoruyi Atekha; Marcus Greiff; Ray Zhang; Luca Carlone
papers.abstract: Geometric foundation models (GFMs) estimate camera mo- tion and scene structure from images without requiring ex- pert parameter tuning, but either lack metric scale or rely on learned priors to infer scale, which is unobservable from monocular images alone. Inertial sensing offers a way to observe metric scale, but existing methods add inertial in- formation through a filter or factor graph, which reintro- duces bespoke parameter tuning and optimization costs that can grow with the trajectory. To bridge this gap, we present AnyVIO, a real-time, feed-forward streaming model for monocular visual-inertial odometry (VIO), which combines a streaming GFM with an inertial foundation model (IFM). Both the GFM and IFM predict the metric motion between consecutive frames, and a lightweight learned fusion head quantifies the reliability of each estimate and blends them in a single forward pass. Across nine datasets recorded from cars, legged and ground robots, and handheld and head- mounted devices, AnyVIO reduces the metric position error of its visual model by 36% while publishing each pose esti- mate 70 ms after an image is received. We further deploy AnyVIO onboard two real vehicles at up to 140 km/h, where it remains accurate in poor lighting and heavy dust.

papers.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
papers.authors: Weihao Cheng
papers.abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

papers.title: Little Red Dots from Primordial Vacuum Bubbles
papers.authors: Miguel Barroso Varela; Katherine Freese; Matthew Kleban; Cameron Norton; Evangelos I. Sfakianakis
papers.abstract: Quantum tunneling transverse to the inflaton trajectory can produce $10^6$--$10^8M_\odot$ primordial black holes at the abundance of JWST's little red dots, without the enhanced curvature perturbations excluded by limits on CMB spectral distortions. Rare vacuum bubbles nucleate during a brief interval of inflation and later form black holes, with adjustable mass and abundance and a narrow mass spectrum of percent-level width. The leading constraint, from accretion, is satisfied for a population matching the bright little red dots even if all the emitted radiation escapes as hard X-rays.

papers.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
papers.authors: Jinbin Luo; Xiaozhe Yao; Shang Yang; Zhijian Liu; Song Han; Qinghao Hu
papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

papers.title: Every galaxy is a radio source: a stellar-mass dependent minimum 150 MHz luminosity identified in the LoTSS Deep Fields
papers.authors: Shravya Shenoy; Daniel J. B. Smith; Martin J. Hardcastle; Soumyadeep Das; Marina I. Arnaudova; Kenneth J. Duncan; Luke R. Holden; Huub J. A. Röttgering
papers.abstract: The second data release of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) Deep Fields includes the deepest wide-field 150 MHz mosaics in existence, covering the ELAIS-N1 field. Combining these radio observations with star-formation rate (SFR) and stellar mass estimates for 113,228 near-infrared selected galaxies derived using Prospector, we re-examine the relationship between galaxies' 150 MHz luminosities ($L_{150\rm{MHz}}$), SFRs and stellar masses. We not only recover the established radio luminosity-SFR relation and its dependence on stellar mass, but also discover a mass-dependent minimum radio luminosity that is independent of SFR. This behaviour is especially evident in galaxies with low specific SFR (sSFR $\equiv$ SFR/$M_*$), at $L_{150\rm MHz} \sim 10^{20}-10^{22}$ W Hz$^{-1}$, where star-forming galaxies are expected to dominate. The non-stellar emission is consistent with low-level accretion onto supermassive black holes (i.e. weak active galactic nuclei, AGN), spanning effective Eddington-scaled accretion rates $λ_{\rm Edd} \sim 10^{-5}-10^{-4}$, suggesting that radio emission due to accretion is widespread and effectively continuous. A two-component model combining star formation- and accretion-driven emission reproduces the observed trends, demonstrating that AGN activity can bias radio-based SFR estimates. The low radio luminosities probed in this work provide a first glimpse of the populations that will be routinely accessible with future facilities such as LOFAR 2.0 and the Square Kilometre Array.

papers.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
papers.authors: Yuxin Jiang; Wenqiang Sun; Jiaqi Li; Yuchao Gu; Lvmin Zhang; Ivor Tsang; Mike Zheng Shou
papers.abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.
